name: Orpiment depilatory paste (vajibt)

lead: Orpiment is a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral. Mixed with slaked lime it forms a paste that dissolves hair at the skin surface, and it is described as still in use for hair removal in rural India.

Jewish tradition credits King Solomon with discovering a depilatory of lime, water and orpiment, and the paste appears in accounts of the Queen of Sheba. The appeal is smooth, hairless skin without shaving or plucking.

paras: Historically the paste was spread on the unwanted hair area and later scraped off with the hair. The same orpiment and lime mixture is also used in tanning to remove hair from hides.
Orpiment is described as extremely toxic and is an arsenic compound. Modern depilatories use other chemistry, such as thiols, which replaced foul-smelling sulfides.

chain: Paste of orpiment and lime applied to hair
Hair breaks down at the skin surface
angle.text: The lime and arsenic sulfide paste removes body hair chemically, leaving the skin smooth. It is a historical and traditional method rather than a modern product.

lead: Orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulfide (As2S3), mixed with about two parts slaked lime (calcium hydroxide), forms a depilatory paste. Wikipedia states the mixture is still commonly used in rural India for hair removal and also in the tanning industry to remove hair from hides.[1]

Jewish lore holds that King Solomon discovered a chemical depilatory made from lime, water and orpiment, as recounted in the Colloquy of the Queen of Sheba from the Aramaic Targum Sheni of Megillat Esther.[2] Classical authors knew depilatory ointments under the name psilothrum.[2]
The look it serves is smooth, hairless skin without shaving, plucking or waxing. No clinical studies of the paste exist, and the mineral's toxicity is the main documented concern.

paras: Orpiment is arsenic sulfide, As2S3, a soft monoclinic mineral whose name comes from Latin auripigmentum, 'gold pigment', for its deep yellow colour.[1] For depilatory use it is mixed with slaked lime in roughly a one-to-two ratio.[1]

Depilatory plasters were known to Greek and Roman authors as psilothrum.[2] In Jewish tradition Solomon is said to have discovered the lime, water and orpiment depilatory.[2] Early sulfide depilatories were later displaced by thiol formulas because of their odour.[2]

Beyond hair removal, orpiment served as a pigment in Egyptian, Chinese and European art and as a Chinese medicine; its use as a pigment declined in the 19th century with cadmium and chromium yellows.[1]
Wikipedia describes orpiment as extremely toxic, and as degrading into arsenic oxides.[1] This is the reason it is documented here as a historical and traditional method.

timeline.event: Depilatory plasters (psilothrum) known to classical authors.[2]
Orpiment declines as a pigment as cadmium and chromium yellows arrive.[1]
